passage:
Mentor note, week 3, Kavitha's delivery project. The problem was that parcels sat at the gate because residents were out at work. Kavitha's new idea is a barter network: neighbours take in each other's parcels and swap favours such as cooking or tutoring. It is a genuinely interesting reframe, and Kavitha pitched it with energy. But when I asked how many neighbours had been asked, the answer was none. Twelve flyers were already printed and a sign-up form was live, yet nobody had discussed trust, such as who holds a key or what happens when a parcel goes missing. Two weeks of effort and the printing money went in before a single neighbour was asked. Next session we will go through what a small first trial would need.

Ankita

qa.q: How many flyers had already been printed?
What might Kavitha be feeling about the barter idea?
qa.a: Kavitha was probably excited and proud of the reframe, given the energy in the pitch.

qa.q: What could Kavitha do instead of printing more materials?
qa.a: Kavitha could ask a few neighbours whether they would trade favours and trust each other with parcels, and try it small before spending more.

qa.q: How might a neighbour who was never asked see the flyer?
qa.a: They might feel unsure or wary, since nobody had explained who holds a key or what happens if a parcel goes missing.

grounding: Shows a clever reframe turned into a full plan without testing whether people would take part or trust it.

passage:
Tuesday night
I think I've cracked it. Delivery in our colony is slow and expensive because every order needs a delivery rider. But what if neighbours delivered for each other? You're going to the market anyway, you carry your neighbour's parcel, and in return someone carries yours. A barter network! No riders, no fees.
Lakshmi, who's been helping with the idea, asked today, "Have you asked anyone if they'd do it?"
I said not yet, but it's obviously good. Who doesn't want free delivery?
She asked what happens if a parcel goes missing. Or someone always takes but never carries. Or people don't want strangers knowing their address.
I said we'd sort those out after launch.
I've already booked a designer for the app logo and spent two weekends on the pitch deck. I'm sure people will love it once they see it.
Thomas

qa.a: A designer for the app logo.

qa.q: How is Thomas feeling about the barter idea?
qa.a: Thomas feels excited and very sure, confident that people will love it once they see it.

qa.q: What would you change first in Thomas's plan?
qa.a: Ask ten neighbours whether they would carry and trust each other's parcels before spending more time or money on the logo and pitch deck.

qa.q: How does Lakshmi see the plan?
qa.a: Lakshmi sees an interesting idea with big untested questions, which is why she keeps asking about missing parcels, fairness and trust.

grounding: It shows a young founder reframing delivery as a neighbour barter network, an interesting idea, but not testing whether people would trade or trust it.
